title: Measure your response time before estimating lost sales
demandReference: UNPAID ORIGINAL INTERNAL SAMPLE. No customer demand or engagement is asserted.
thumbnailBrief: Original typography: HOW LONG DO LEADS WAIT? Use a clock and a blank measurement sheet, not revenue figures.

competitors.gap: Original educational measurement example; channel performance was not evaluated.

scenes.narration: How long does a new inquiry wait for your first reply? Measure that before estimating what a delay costs.
scenes.visual: Original animated clock beside an empty response log.
scenes.rightsReference: Original ULTRON text and native shapes; no third-party footage.
scenes.caption: Measure reply time first

scenes.narration: Record when each authorized inquiry arrived and when someone replied. Keep customer details private. Separate business hours from overnight waits.
scenes.visual: Original table with column labels only: received, replied, business hours.
scenes.rightsReference: Original ULTRON table; no customer data or invented measurements.
scenes.caption: Record received and replied times

scenes.narration: Review unanswered inquiries and compare the same time periods. A response-time change is an observation. It does not by itself prove extra sales.
scenes.visual: Original comparison diagram marked observation, not a revenue forecast.
scenes.caption: An observation is not proof of extra sales

scenes.narration: Choose one practical reply improvement and measure again. Start with the records you already have permission to use.
scenes.visual: Original checklist: record, review, improve, measure again.
scenes.caption: Choose one improvement. Measure again.
